video.title: This Kid Sells a CRAZY Amount of Burgers ($1.4M/Year)...How?!

summary: Henry describes building Smashers from a food trailer into a burger restaurant in Norfolk, Virginia, and explains its menu, costs, marketing, staffing, suppliers, and growth plans. He says the restaurant did about $1.45 million in 2025 and is projected to do $1.7 million this year. His path included experimenting with burgers at home, testing the concept in a trailer, then opening a second-generation restaurant space. The interview also covers setbacks, including a costly commissary kitchen and a food truck he plans to phase out.

speakers.description: The host is addressed as Paul in the transcript; the name is inferred from that address.

speakers.name: Dylan McCong

ideas.name: Smashers burger restaurant
ideas.one_liner: A simple-menu smash burger restaurant that sells burgers, fresh-cut fries, and milkshakes.
ideas.business_model: In-person restaurant sales plus online orders through the restaurant's website and app and third-party platforms.
ideas.customer: People who want burgers, fries, and milkshakes; the restaurant is in Norfolk, Virginia.
ideas.problem: Not stated as a customer problem; Henry describes the concept as perfecting simplicity and says he believes the product is superior to Five Guys.
ideas.offer: Smash burgers, fresh-cut fries, and hand-scooped ice cream milkshakes, with a simple menu and customizable toppings.

pricing.model: Per-item food and drink sales; meal bundles are also offered.

price_points.label: Double burger; transcript says “a 99,” so the full price is unclear

pricing.notes: The transcript does not clearly preserve the double burger price.

acquisition_channels.details: The restaurant posts a daily reel on four platforms. It developed a raw, humorous, anti-corporate style. A staged robbery video brought new customers.

quote.text: We had a robbery skit. So we had somebody I put on a shasty ski mask and we took my camera footage and we screwed record of it, faking a robbery.
quote.speaker: Henry

acquisition_channels.details: They previously used Facebook Meta ads by promoting the best-performing food video as a local ad.

quote.text: We have in the past on just Facebook meta ads. So we'll try to take the best performing food video and run it as a local ad.
quote.speaker: Henry

acquisition_channels.details: The first restaurant location had strong visibility at a popular intersection. Henry says the initial burger market on a beachfront had no food vendors.

ideas.delivery: Restaurant staff cook burgers and fries to order and assemble meals. Henry says the average ticket time is about three to four minutes. Online orders are placed through the restaurant website and app and through third-party delivery platforms.
unit_economics_claims: Henry says monthly revenue is about $120,000, with 75% from in-restaurant customers and 25% from online orders.
He says prime costs should ideally be around 56%, burger cost of goods should stay below 30%, and burger cost before toppings should not exceed 25%.
He says fries and drinks produce most of the restaurant's profit.
He says the original location's rent is almost $7,000 per month.
He says 2025 revenue was about $1.45 million and projects $1.7 million this year.
ideas.startup_cost: The restaurant cost about $550,000 to open. Henry says funding included a personal loan, remaining food trailer profits, and a tenant improvement allowance.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The restaurant opened after about four summers of running the food trailer. Henry says the restaurant's first month was about $35,000–$40,000 in sales.

acquisition.how: Agents can draft and schedule posts and help test ad creative, with a person filming, approving brand-sensitive humor, and checking local ad targeting.

onboarding.how: Ordering can be digital, but staff still handle customer questions, exceptions, and restaurant service.

delivery.how: People must cook, assemble, and hand over food; physical restaurant work cannot be unattended by software.

billing.how: Online ordering and card payments can be processed by software, but cash handling, refunds, and reconciliation need routine human checks.

support.how: Software could handle common order questions, but service issues and food complaints require staff judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: The restaurant model can work in the UK, but the transcript's prices, suppliers, and operating figures are US-specific. A UK operator would need to adapt food safety, employment, planning, and local licensing practices.

risks: Food service requires people on site to prepare and serve products, so it is a poor fit for a founder seeking near-unattended operation.
Henry says the costs of goods and labour are the two largest costs and that beef prices rose from about $3.40 to almost $5 per pound.
A second food truck had lower sales volume and was harder to manage.
Staged crime-themed marketing can confuse the public or create reputational problems if viewers mistake it for a real event.

tactics.name: Validate the burger before committing to a restaurant
steps: Make the product repeatedly at home and refine individual details.
Use friends and family requests as an early signal that people may pay for it.
Test the concept in a food trailer before signing a brick-and-mortar lease.

quote.text: I like the food truck just because you can really test your concept before you make a massive decision like signing a lease on a brick and mortar spot.
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Learn restaurant operations by working across shifts
steps: Henry took a short job at Five Guys and worked a day shift, mid shifts, and a night shift to observe operations.
He later hired the manager he had worked under as Smashers' general manager.

quote.text: I joined it intentionally, I called it Operation Trojan Burger, so I did a day shift, a mid shift, two mid shifts, and then a night shift
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Look for second-generation restaurant sites
steps: Prefer a site previously used as a restaurant to reduce the amount of work needed.
Check visibility and whether customers can enter and exit easily.
Review household income and population within one-, three-, and five-mile radii.
Use an experienced real estate agent when reviewing the lease.

quote.text: When looking for your first restaurant, you wanna make sure that's a second generation restaurant, the previous tenant to this was Fat Burger
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Keep the menu simple and control food costs
steps: Start with a narrow menu and add items only after the operation is established.
Track cost of goods and weekly inventory.
Compare suppliers and product quality instead of assuming the current vendor has the best deal.
Negotiate supplier pricing when buying power gives you leverage.

quote.text: First things first, I'll keep my menu simple. I like the food truck just because you can really test your concept
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Build a repeatable content routine
steps: Post one reel daily across four platforms.
Use a distinctive, humorous, raw style instead of repeating common food trends.
Review which food videos perform best and use those as local paid ads.
Have a dedicated content creator handle filming and editing, with the owner contributing ideas and appearing on camera.

quote.text: Yeah, so currently we do predominantly social media marketing. We do a daily reel on four platforms. We had little to no success in the beginning
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Use operating systems to set expectations
steps: Write policies and processes that tell staff what to do.
Use checklists for recurring tasks such as putting up umbrellas in the morning.
Make the company process the source of instructions rather than relying on informal verbal requests.

quote.text: So if I have a checklist that tells somebody to put up umbrellas in the morning as opposed to me saying it, they're much more likely to do it.
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Review vendor options and negotiate with leverage
steps: Compare distributors against the products and brands the menu requires.
Build a working relationship with the account representative but verify invoices and prices.
Use credible alternative suppliers and multi-location buying power to negotiate.

quote.text: If you're ignorant and you don't explore your options, they will oftentimes take advantage of that. It's important to have strong relationships in this business
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Avoid adding fixed costs on impulse
steps: Check whether a new space or asset has enough business volume to pay for itself.
Separate a practical operating need from a desire to prove the business is successful.
Henry says the commissary would need about three locations to justify making and distributing sauce from it.

quote.text: I made this decision mainly on impulse. I think it was about seven months at the running of the restaurant and became very successful.
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Protect the brand early
steps: Check trademark availability and secure the name before investing heavily in branding.
Gather intellectual property rights early if the brand has meaningful value.

quote.text: Trademarks, so are the priority. Make sure that you're legal and secure. And then if you have a lot of branding around your name
quote.speaker: Henry

tactics.name: Take action and learn from mistakes
steps: Make decisions, review what happened, and apply the learning to the next decision.
Henry says speed of execution mattered more to him than trying to avoid every wrong decision.

quote.text: So like, while somebody is staying still, I'm gonna make five wrong decisions, look like a fool, but I'll end up at the sixth right decision before they even move.
quote.speaker: Henry

warnings.warning: Henry says he made the commissary decision on impulse, partly from ego, and calls it his biggest waste of money yet.
Henry says the food truck consumes 30%–40% of his time and is less profitable than the restaurant, so he plans to phase it out.
He says he initially tracked finances by looking at his bank balance at the beginning and end of summer, rather than systematically tracking the numbers.
Henry says suppliers may take advantage of operators who do not compare options or check prices and invoices.
Henry says early staff turnover was high because he did not set expectations well as he added responsibilities.
The robbery video was staged, but the transcript describes news-style footage of a masked person entering the kitchen. Viewers could mistake staged content for a real event.
The host includes promotional reads for Busy and an UpFlip business assessment test. These create promotional context; Busy is specifically presented as a sponsor.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is the operator and gives concrete operating processes, supplier details, and business figures. The figures are self-reported, several are estimates or projections, and the local Whisper transcript contains garbled names and amounts.
